planting.note: Divide established clumps or plant container stock in early spring into fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from cold, drying winds.

directions: Set divisions into fertile, moisture-retentive soil enriched with leaf mold, in partial shade away from harsh winter wind. Orange Queen is a selection of the warleyense hybrid prized for its unusually vivid burnt-orange sepals paired with smaller pale yellow petals, carried in airy sprays above the foliage in mid to late spring. New leaflets emerge with a coppery-red flush before settling into mid-green for summer, giving the clump a second season of interest. Cut back old foliage in late winter just before the flower spikes rise so the color show is not obscured by the previous year's leaves.

planting.note: Divide dormant clumps or plant container-grown stock in early spring into cool, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Grow in reliably moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where this Japanese-bred selection is named for its frilly, peacock-like blooms. Beni-kujaku produces wavy-petaled flowers whose sepals and petals are nearly equal in size, giving a full, almost double-flowered look in rosy pink shading to a pale center as the small leaflets unfurl alongside them in early spring. Foliage is often lightly edged in red when young before maturing to green, adding understated texture through summer. Established clumps tolerate dry shade reasonably well but bloom and foliage color are both best with consistent moisture during spring growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from drying wind.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, where Tamabotan opens nodding, silvery-lavender flowers in early spring just as the heart-shaped leaflets emerge deep purple before fading to turquoise and then green. Because its sepals, petals, and spurs are all nearly the same length, the flower reads as a soft, rounded double rather than the typical spidery epimedium bloom. The first flush of spring foliage stays low at around eight inches, then a second summer flush of leaves can rise considerably taller, so allow room for that later growth when siting it. Mulch lightly each fall to protect the shallow rhizomes and sustain the moisture this cultivar prefers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade, though established plants tolerate considerably more sun than most hellebores.

directions: Site this sterile niger x corsicus hybrid in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, though it is noticeably more sun-tolerant than Christmas rose itself and can take considerable direct light in cooler climates. Green Corsican is an unusually robust, semi-evergreen selection producing branched stems of flattish, creamy white flowers centered by a prominent boss of yellow stamens from late winter into early spring. Its leathery, divided foliage stays handsome through the growing season and resists the leaf spot that troubles many hellebores. Because it sets no viable seed, propagate only by division of established clumps every few years in late summer.

scientific_name: Helleborus x nigercors 'HGC Ice Breaker Fancy'

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Grow in moist but well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, where this Gold Collection selection tolerates more direct light than most hellebores thanks to its Corsican parentage. Ice Breaker Fancy carries outward-facing, creamy white flowers from winter into spring that age gradually to soft green with a pink blush along the petal edges and reverse, extending the display well past typical bloom time. Glossy, dark green, spiny-toothed evergreen foliage forms a tidy clump that stays attractive year-round. As a sterile interspecific hybrid it produces no self-sown seedlings, so increase the planting only through division of mature clumps.
